subject: ezPerm and same seed for permutations

messages.author: 13900a48eddf519a
messages.subject: ezPerm and same seed for permutations
parts:
Dear Mike and ez users,

I am using ezPerm on my data. I noticed this week that, with the same dataset and the same number of permutation, I always obtained the same results. I think that it is linked to the use of the same seed for permutations.
According to the sources, I think that the initialisation of the seed is made by "set.seed(this_perm)" (with this_perm equal to the number of permutation in progress), which confirms my hypothesis.

I thought (but maybe I am wrong) that to run statistics with permutations, you need to change your seed at each time. Is there a statistical reason about always using the same seed?


Thank you very much

With all the best,
Evelyne Duvernois

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] ezPerm and same seed for permutations
parts:
I guess it could be useful to re-run the permutation test a couple times using different seeds to confirm that you're getting approximately the same result (if you didn't, you'd want to increase the number of iterations). 

The code's current behaviour of setting a new seed on every iteration is certainly useless; I can't see why I did it that way! I should re-code it to set the seed at the beginning based on an argument that defaults to 1 for replicability but that the user can change to achieve the above check.

messages.subject: Re: [ez4r] ezPerm and same seed for permutations
parts:
Dear Mike

Thank you for your answer.

Indeed, I have tested with different seeds. I have just modified line 107 from your sources with: set.seed(as.integer((as.double(Sys.time())*1000+Sys.getpid()) %% 2^31))
And I obtained different results (of course marginal).

I think that many package runs like that:
- if you do all permutations (exact test), you don't care about the order of permutations. And you will obtain the same results all the time.
- if you need to approximate (monte carlo), you have to realize permutations but not the same permutations all the time. In that context, you need to change the seed.

Am I wrong?

Le mercredi 8 juin 2016 15:40:54 UTC+2, Mike Lawrence a écrit :
I guess it could be useful to re-run the permutation test a couple times using different seeds to confirm that you're getting approximately the same result (if you didn't, you'd want to increase the number of iterations).
